title: Students’ Voices on Generative AI: Perceptions, Benefits, and Challenges in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how university students perceive generative AI technologies such as ChatGPT in higher education. The study asks three main questions: how familiar students are with generative AI, what benefits and challenges they perceive in using it for teaching and learning, and how it might be effectively integrated into higher education. The paper is framed by Biggs’ 3P model, emphasizing that students’ perceptions of learning environments and tools can influence learning approaches and outcomes.

The study used an online survey with both closed-ended and open-ended questions, making it a mixed-methods observational study. The survey covered knowledge of generative AI, willingness to use it, concerns about its use, and perceived effects on teaching and learning. Students described a range of uses for generative AI, including personalized learning support, writing and brainstorming assistance, research and analysis support, multimedia generation, and administrative help. Reported perceived benefits included immediate feedback, tailored support, efficiency, idea generation, and support for self-directed learning.

Participants were 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students from multiple disciplines across post-secondary institutions in Hong Kong. The sample included students from ten faculties, with both STEM and non-STEM representation. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlations, and thematic analysis of open-ended responses. The study was conducted through an online questionnaire rather than a classroom intervention, and it focused on student perceptions rather than measured learning outcomes.

The main conclusion is that students generally held positive attitudes toward generative AI and saw strong potential for personalized support, writing help, brainstorming, and research assistance. At the same time, they expressed substantial concerns about accuracy, transparency, privacy, plagiarism, over-reliance, reduced critical thinking and creativity, and broader impacts on careers and human values. The authors argue that institutions should support responsible integration of generative AI through AI literacy education, clearer policies, and safeguards around ethics, privacy, and transparency.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey with descriptive, correlational, and qualitative thematic analyses of student perceptions. It is empirical and peer-reviewed, but it does not estimate causal effects of GenAI on learning outcomes and relies on self-report data from a convenience sample.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports mostly perceived benefits and concerns rather than measured learning impacts, and no intervention effect sizes on academic outcomes are provided. Impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated as positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Survey study of university students' perceptions of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT for personalized learning support, brainstorming, assignment help, feedback, and research assistance.

Students describe using generative AI for writing assistance including brainstorming, grammar/paraphrasing help, polishing articles, feedback on drafts, and second-language vocabulary/text generation support.

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived generative AI positively for literacy-related tasks such as brainstorming, writing improvement, grammar/paraphrasing, and feedback on drafts, based on survey responses from n=399 Hong Kong university students. However, these are self-reported perceptions rather than measured reading/writing gains, and students also expressed concerns about plagiarism, inaccurate content, and reduced independent thinking; no causal learning effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceptions of GenAI usefulness for writing, brainstorming, and feedback via online survey and open-ended responses

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally positive attitudes toward GenAI, including willingness to integrate it into learning practices (Mean=3.85, SD=1.02) and belief that it can improve motivation and support learning independently. Perceived willingness to use GenAI was positively correlated with knowledge of GenAI (r=0.189, p<0.001) and frequency of use (r=0.326, p<0.001), though this reflects attitudes and intentions rather than observed behavioral outcomes.
finding.measure: Survey ratings of willingness, attitudes, and perceived motivational/support benefits

finding.finding_summary: Students expressed concern that GenAI may undermine critical thinking, creativity, and transferable skills, with concern items showing moderate endorsement: undermines value of university education (Mean=3.15, SD=1.17), hinders development of generic/transferable skills (Mean=3.10, SD=1.23), and over-reliance concerns (Mean=2.85, SD=1.13). These findings are based on perceptions rather than direct assessments of skill decline, but the paper substantively centers these risks as a challenge of implementation.
finding.measure: Survey items and qualitative responses on critical thinking, creativity, over-reliance, and transferable skills

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived GenAI as improving efficiency by saving time (Mean=4.20, SD=0.82), providing 24/7 availability (Mean=4.12, SD=0.83), and supporting faster completion of writing, research, and administrative tasks. Qualitative responses emphasized immediate answers, rapid feedback, literature summarization, and help with repetitive work, but no objective productivity or workload metrics were collected.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceptions of time saving, availability, and efficiency benefits from survey and open-ended responses

finding.finding_summary: The study identified substantial institutional implications around policy, ethics, privacy, academic integrity, and future curriculum design. Students were moderately concerned that GenAI use undermines the value of university education (Mean=3.15, SD=1.17), and qualitative responses highlighted plagiarism, transparency, privacy, and teacher-student relationship concerns alongside support for institutional AI literacy training and policy development.
finding.measure: Survey concern items and thematic analysis of open-ended responses about policy, ethics, privacy, and educational value
